newsitem.title: INDONESIA: SE Asian Grain - Indonesia washes out corn deals.
newsitem.headline: SE Asian Grain - Indonesia washes out corn deals.

text.p: Domestic grain prices in Southeast Asia generallly remained soft this week with some Indonesian importers washing out contracts for up to 70,000 tonnes of corn, traders said on Wednesday.

But regional soymeal prices were steady to firmer, particularly in Thailand where prices continued to rise as Thai feedmillers delayed imports on expectations the government will lift import quotas, or at least cut tariffs for imported animal feed, trade and industry sources in Bangkok said.

"I hear there have been a number of washouts of last quarter delivery corn," said one Indonesian trader, who estimated the total at up to 70,000 tonnes. "Some made money while others lost some," he added.
Another trader said the Indonesian washouts were mostly with U.S. sellers and added that local players were unlikely to enter into new corn contracts for delivery this year.
"Some players made good margins (in the washouts) and will be looking to buy corn locally as harvests are expected to continue until December," the trader said.
Corn was quoted at 390-400 rupiah a kg in Jakarta, compared with 420 rupiah a week ago.
A trader in the key corn growing region of Lampung in South Sumatra said demand from Jakarta had been weak and that he had been selling mostly to players in Palembang.
"I heard there had been offers from Vietnam at $160 a tonne (C&F) but I don't know if there had been any takers," he said.
Domestic Indonesian soymeal prices firmed to around 850 rupiah a kg, up from 820-830 rupiah last week, due to tight supplies from producers such as India and Argentina.
"Cargo is becoming hard to get from India. Getting even 250 tonnes per day seems to be difficult," one trader said.
Grain prices in Malaysia were unchanged and local dealers did not report any significant activity.
But a Singapore-based trader confirmed he had done a sale of 25,000 tonnes of South American soymeal to a Malaysian buyer for October/November shipment at $304 a tonne C&F.
"That's about the only thing that happened on the Malaysian side last week. All other grains were quiet," the trader said.
Aside from the deal with Malaysia, the trader said Vietnam bought 25,000 tonnes of Australian wheat for October shipment at $202 a tonne C&F.
He said corn and wheat trade was slow ahead of a key crop report to be issued by the United States Agriculture Department (USDA) later this month.
"This report will have the July/August/September crop data and we could see more buying next week if production falls," said the trader.
One Kuala Lumpur flour mill official said he had halted his purchases to await the new USDA data.
"The market is usually the same this time of the year with the crop in the U.S. being harvested," said the official. "I think I'll wait for a clearer signal."

"A" grade wheat in bags was quoted at 840 ringgit a tonne ex-factory/godown central region. Low-grade wheat was at 550-600 ringgit. Local soymeal was quoted at 818.46 ringgit a tonne, while imported soymeal was going for about 780-800 ringgit. Bulk corn was at 550 ringgit ex-factory/godown in the central region.
In Thailand, tight supplies boosted the price of soymeal to around 10.45 baht a kg from 10.30-10.40 a kg last week.
Corn prices were stable to lower as the industry awaited fresh supplies from the new crop.
Prices of silo grade corn were quoted at 4.25-4.30 baht a kg from 4.30-4.50 baht a kg last week. Feed grade corn was quoted at 4.60 baht a kg, barely changed from last week.

The only import order confirmed by trade sources was the one made last week by a local feed producer who bought 15,000 tonnes of soybeans from the U.S. for October shipment. The price was said to be $335 a tonne C&F Bangkok.
"Besides that, we heard nothing. That's why local soymeal prices continue to rise," said one trader.

The impending arrival of U.S. corn gluten meal next week and cargoes of soymeal from Brazil and Argentina later this month would give feed producers, already pinched by tight supplies, some room to wait, traders said.
